Recap

items.item: every time series is uniquely identified by its metric name and optional key-value pairs called labels; the change of any label's value, including adding or removing labels, creates a new time series

at.step: Reveal: a series is its metric name plus its full label set

items.item: every unique combination of key-value label pairs represents a new time series; do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality

at.step: Hook: one label, and the server gets killed
Reveal: one unbounded label multiplies every series it touches

items.item: postings sections store monotonically increasing lists of series references that contain a given label pair, with an offset table sorted by label name and value

at.step: Reveal: a postings intersection skips most series; a regex can't
Reveal: a scan-based model has no per-series index to blow up

items.item: A one-line label addition isn't a small change to a dashboard query — it's a change to the identity rule of every series the pipeline tracks, which is why its blast radius is the whole metrics server, not one chart.

at.step: Hook: one label, and the server gets killed

items.item: Calling two readings 'the same series' or 'different series' isn't a judgment call — it's settled entirely by whether their label sets are identical, which is why a system can define cardinality exactly instead of estimating it.

at.step: Reveal: a series is its metric name plus its full label set

items.item: The gap between a worst-case cross product and the actual series count isn't noise to be ignored — it's the measurable effect of real-world constraints (not every sensor fits every piece of equipment) that a naive multiplication can't see.

at.step: Reveal: worst-case cross product vs. the plant's own actual series count

items.item: The honest answer to whether a multi-label query must scan every series is 'it depends on the matcher,' not a single yes or no — an equality matcher and a regex matcher are different problems with different costs, even inside the same query language.

at.step: Predict: does a multi-label query have to scan every series?

items.item: A postings intersection being cheap and a regex scan being expensive aren't two separate facts about two different systems — they're the same index's structure helping one access pattern and offering nothing to the other.

at.step: Reveal: a postings intersection skips most series; a regex can't

items.item: An unbounded label doesn't make the system slow — it makes the number of things the system has to track literally unbounded, which is a qualitatively different failure than a system merely running slower under load.

at.step: Reveal: one unbounded label multiplies every series it touches

items.item: A scan-based model doesn't avoid the cardinality problem — it changes which operation gets expensive, trading an index that can blow up for a scan that's merely proportional to data size, which is a real trade, not a free win.

at.step: Reveal: a scan-based model has no per-series index to blow up

items.item: Choosing between a per-series index and a scan-based engine is a decision about which queries you expect to run, not a decision about which architecture is objectively better — a point-lookup-heavy workload and a high-cardinality analytical workload want opposite answers.

at.step: Recap

items.item: A batch or lot ID belongs in a fact table joined to a series, not inside the series' own identity, because a fact table's rows can grow without bound while a series identity's growth is exactly what the system has to index.

at.step: Recap

items.item: Counting the series before and after a schema change, and being able to say exactly where the new series count came from, is what turns 'our memory usage exploded' from a mystery into an arithmetic fact anyone can check.
